name: Windsurfing
seoDesc: Windsurfing: work out sail size (Sail) from the wind speed and the width. A free sports calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the wind speed, the width and the depth and the Windsurfing calculator solves for sail size (Sail). That makes it useful for a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Windsurfing calculator work?
sections.html:
The Windsurfing calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports sail size (Sail) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the board type and the fin/Board type); then you type in the wind speed, the width (Board), the depth (2) and the depth (3).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• I want a sail for: pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as beginners and planing. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Wind speed: a measured quantity, entered by default in knots. The unit chip switches it to any of the 25 supported units.
  • Board type: pick the option that matches your case — 7 options, such as beginner Board, cruising Longboard and first Shortboard. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Width (Board): a measured quantity, entered by default in centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • Fin/Board type: pick the option that matches your case — 5 options, such as freeride / Slalom, wave and formula. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Depth (2): a measured quantity, entered by default in centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • Depth (3): a measured quantity, entered by default in centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • Depth (9): a measured quantity, entered by default in centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • Depth (10): a measured quantity, entered by default in centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • Area: a measured quantity, entered by default in square centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 24 supported units.
  • Area (2): a measured quantity, entered by default in square centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 24 supported units.
  • J: a plain number with no unit attached.

7 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Windsurfing calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Sail size=(67 ÷ 50) × sailor weight ÷ wind speed
Sail size=(31 ÷ 50) × sailor weight ÷ wind speed
Volume=(217 ÷ 100) × sailor weight + 217 ÷ 10
Sailor weight=(100 ÷ 33) × width − 5600 ÷ 33
Sailor weight=(25 ÷ 22) × length − 250
Volume=(44 ÷ 25) × sailor weight + 90

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
The form opens with a complete set of values: I want a sail for set to beginners, Wind speed = 19 kn, Board type set to Beginner Board and Fin/Board type set to Freeride / Slalom. Straight away the calculator returns B = 1, C = 1, G = 1 and F = 1.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: B = 1, C = 1, G = 1 and F = 1 should be roughly the size you expected from I want a sail for set to beginners and Wind speed = 19 kn.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Sailor weight: Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Wind speed: Speed, opening in knots
  • Sail size (Sail): Area, opening in square meters
  • Sail size (Sail): Area, opening in square meters
  • Sail size (Sail): Area, opening in square meters
  • Volume (Board): Volume, opening in liters
  • Width (Board): Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length (Board): Length, opening in centimeters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Windsurfing calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the wind speed, the width and the depth — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Windsurfing calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns sail size (Sail), derived from the wind speed, the width and the depth. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Windsurfing calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the wind speed, the width and the depth, which is 12 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter sailor weight in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Sailor weight opens in kilograms and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (7 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports B = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Windsurfing calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
